newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets watch US/local data.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets watch US/local data.

text.p: Australian debt and equity markets are expected to move in line with their U.S. cousins in the early part of the week following a torrid Friday session in New York where strong labour force data showed that the economy remains turbo-charged.

U.S. bonds slumped in reaction to the July employment report which showed that the number of new jobs was way above expectations and a fall in the unemployment rate to a 24-year low of 4.8 percent. This data, along with a strong NAPM report, raised the spectre of another Fed rate hike later in the year.

Wall Street mostly shrugged off the economic data to end Friday with only slight losses after an earlier free-fall. The U.S. dollar ended at eight-year highs against the mark, driven by expectations of higher rates.
Once the U.S. data has been absorbed by traders, the focus will switch to local economic figures later in the week, analysts said.
Also, the Reserve Bank holds its monthly board meeting on Tuesday but it will hold no surprises following last week's 50 basis point cut in the official cash rate.

The board meeting this week has been rendered an anticlimax, but July labour force and June housing finance data on Thursday and Friday this week will help formulate market opinion on the prospect of another rate cut.
Generally, economists see another rate cut as unlikely after five easings in 12 months of half a percentage point each.
A Reuters survey on Friday found a median forecast of a 30 percent chance of another rate cut -- but the data this week is expected to be weak and may be encouraging for those looking for a rate cut.
Employment is expected to have risen by 25,000 in July but even after the 11,900 rise in June it will not be enough to reverse the 40,300 fall in May.

With the participation expected to rise, after falling over the last three months, unemployment is seen edging back over 8.5 percent. Economists said ANZ job advertisements for July will provide a longer-term clue to the direction of employmnent growth than the monthly data from the ABS to be issued three days later.

Housing finance is expected to post its second successive sizeable fall -- which when combined with softness in the retail sector -- suggests that the economy has slowed into the middle of the year and has left the door open for a possible sixth rate cut.

Macquarie Bank said in preview of the two key data releases that unemployment was expected to rise to 8.7 percent and that housing finance was expected to have fallen by six percent in June, despite a more confident market consensus which predicts a 2.5 percent rise. The data showed an 8.4 percent fall in May.
"If growth fails to pick up as expected, another official rate cut cannot be ruled out -- particularly in the absence of other policy responses to high unemployment," Macquarie said.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (10-yr yield Fri close 6.34 pct, -0.06)

The Australian bond market will start the week with a very soft tone following the exceptionally strong U.S. employment report for July which showed a jump in the number of new jobs and a fall in the jobless rate to a 24-year low.
The yield on the key U.S. 30-year benchmark government bond ended at 6.45 percent from 6.30 percent on Thursday.

However, Monday's local reaction will be slightly distorted with the state of New South Wales closed for a bank holiday and the Sydney Futures Exchange trading floor closed. Trading of all futures instruments will be available through the screen-based SYCOM system.
The U.S. market is likely to call the tune for local debt in the first part of this week and until Thursday's release of Australia's own labour force report.
"If this (local data) proves to weak again, it will start talk again of another easing," one trader said.

Ten-year bonds hit their lowest level for nearly a quarter of a century last week at below 6.35 percent following the Reserve Bank's 1/2 point rate cut, weak building approvals and a weaker-than-expected set of monthly and quarterly retail trade data.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri close NYK: US$0.7390, SYD US$0.7440)

The Australian dollar ended last week at the upper end of recent trading ranges despite the fact official cash rates had been cut below those in the U.S. for the first time since financial markets here were deregulated in the early 1980s.

The move had been so well priced in that the reaction largely involved short covering, although analysts thought it bearish that the currency never came close to testing chart resistance at US$0.7530/50.

Much of the equanimity was due to expectations the easing was the last of the cycle, but dire data on retail sales and building approvals made some wonder if this outlook was as premature as that which saw a strong pickup in the first half of this year.

And the omens are not promising for this week as private banking data suggests housing finance figures Friday will show a fall in commitments of around 5.0 percent in June on top of a surprise 8.4 percent drop the month before.

Neither were analysts confident July jobs data Thursday will show the recovery in employment so long anticipated. Forecasts favour a rise of around 25,000 which even combined with June's 11,900 gain will still not make up for May's fall of 40,300.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (All Ords Fri close: 2,727.5, - 7.6)
The corporate reporting season is the near term focus for the equity market with little else, bar dramatic downward moves on Wall Street, to capture traders imagination.
"Results are the next thing coming around. Analysts are not doing much at the moment -- there is no point doing anything until the new data comes out," said a Brisbane-based dealer.
A bank holiday on Monday is likely to dampen institutional participation and investor enthusiasm until later in the week.
"It's bank holiday on Monday so a lot of the institutional investors will be off," said a Sydney broker.

Some hope was held for further benefit from last Wednesday's interest rate cut with traders saying the market had failed to fully digest the rate reduction, noting the lags that usually applied to such policy easings.
However, they added the market remained well underpinned by the current low interest rate environment.

"We still haven't seen the market appreciation of the effect on our economy of cut in the interest rate. Provided we get a reasonable lead from Wall Street, we'll have a good week," said broker Kevin Lourey of Peake Lands Kirwan.
Coca-Cola Amatil Ltd half year results on Wednesday represent the bluechip highlight, while television and film production group Southern Star Group Ltd has its annual meeting on Tuesday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
